summary:
Amazon Pulse is an interactive, browser-based 3D geospatial dashboard built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Dancing with the SARs) that tracks monthly deforestation, flooded forests, and open water across key Amazon hotspots.

To solve the challenge of persistent tropical cloud cover that blinds traditional optical satellites, Amazon Pulse fuses NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar with Sentinel-1 C-band radar and independent Sentinel-2 optical and RADD evidence onto a unified 20-meter grid. Its automated verification pipeline assigns multi-sensor confidence scores to each candidate patch, effectively separating true structural canopy loss from seasonal flood dynamics and false radar alarms.

This project is vital because single-sensor alerts often suffer from noise and misclassifications. By delivering lightweight, serverless analytics via MapLibre 3D, Amazon Pulse empowers researchers, conservationists, and journalists with rapid, transparent, and verifiable forest intelligence without requiring heavy backend infrastructure.
details:
What it does / how it works

Amazon Pulse is an interactive web dashboard designed to help people visualize and understand forest change in the Amazon using radar-based satellite data. The project combines Sentinel-1 C-band radar, NISAR L-band radar, and additional evidence such as Sentinel-2 optical imagery, NDVI vegetation loss, RADD alerts, slope data, and water masks.

The system detects likely deforestation and environmental change by comparing monthly radar patterns against reference baselines. It then validates those detections using independent signals to estimate confidence. Areas that appear to be undergoing forest clearance, flooded forest change, or open water expansion are displayed as interactive hotspots on a map. Users can swipe between before/after views, explore 3D terrain, inspect specific patches, and view time-series charts for each affected area.

The app is designed to make complex remote sensing information understandable in a visual, accessible way. Instead of only showing raw data, it turns outputs into a story: where change is happening, when it started, how likely it is to be real, and what additional evidence supports or questions the finding.

Benefits

This project helps people quickly identify and interpret signs of ecosystem disturbance, including deforestation and flood-related forest change. It reduces the amount of technical expertise needed to understand SAR-based monitoring by presenting the results through an intuitive map interface with interactive controls.

It also offers a strong educational benefit. By combining radar science with visual storytelling, the project helps non-specialists understand how satellites detect environmental change, why multiple signals are important, and how confident we are in a detection.

Intended impact

The intended impact is to support environmental awareness, monitoring, and decision-making by making change detection more accessible. In a region as large and ecologically important as the Amazon, tools like this can help researchers, communities, educators, and decision-makers identify high-risk areas and better understand where and when forest loss or floodplain change is occurring.

At a broader level, the project aims to contribute to public understanding of climate and biodiversity risk and to demonstrate how open Earth observation data can be used to monitor vulnerable ecosystems.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software used

This project uses a combination of cloud geospatial analysis, Python processing, and frontend web visualization:

  • Sentinel-1 radar data
  • NISAR L-band data
  • Sentinel-2 optical imagery
  • Google Earth Engine for large-scale geospatial processing
  • Python for data retrieval and site generation
  • Libraries such as rasterio, h5py, numpy, scipy, requests, and Pillow
  • MapLibre GL JS for the interactive map interface
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the web experience

Static hosting for the final site, so no server-side computation is required when viewing the results

The project is primarily software-based, but it depends heavily on satellite data from NASA, ESA, and other Earth observation sources. No specialized physical hardware was required beyond a standard laptop or development workstation.

How it is creative

The project is creative in the way it turns scientific data into an interactive, story-driven visual experience. Rather than presenting a flat map of detections, it builds a narrative around change: a hotspot becomes a place you can inspect, compare, and understand over time.

The use of 3D terrain, before/after comparison, guided tours, colour-coded time-series trends, and confidence filters makes the product engaging and educational. It transforms complex environmental monitoring into an experience that is both informative and visually compelling.

The project also creatively combines different sensor types to explain the science behind the findings. Seeing how C-band and L-band data complement each other gives the project a strong, visually intuitive storytelling approach.

Factors the team considered

Several important factors shaped the project design:

Data reliability: Radar signals can be noisy or ambiguous, so the team used multiple lines of evidence to improve confidence and reduce false alarms.

Accessibility: The interface was built to be understandable to general users, not just remote sensing experts.

Performance: Since the project is meant to be interactive, the heavy processing was separated from the final viewer, using pre-generated outputs for fast browsing.

Environmental relevance: The project focused on a critical global issue—Amazon forest change and floodplain dynamics—where timely interpretation matters.

Scientific transparency: The project clearly communicates that detections are candidate alerts and not field-verified proof of deforestation.

Usability: The dashboard includes filters, hotspot summaries, and guided exploration to help users navigate a large amount of geospatial information.

Overall, Amazon Pulse combines science, data visualization, and environmental storytelling to make large-scale satellite monitoring more understandable, useful, and impactful.
